h1: AC Repair in Third Ward, Houston
title: AC Repair Third Ward, Houston | AC Repair Houston
description: Cottages and infill on narrow lots with almost no shade, where the sun loads the walls and the equipment has been patched for decades.
intro: Third Ward sits on some of the oldest continuously settled ground in Houston, and the cooling calls there tend to start with the building rather than the machine. Cottages from the 1930s through the 1950s sit shoulder to shoulder on narrow lots where the street trees stop at the sidewalk, so the roof, the back wall and the driveway concrete take a full afternoon of sun. Throw in 1960s and 1970s infill and a repair history that runs longer than most marriages, and what you have is a house whose system was never matched to it.
localAngle: Most of the housing was framed between 1930 and 1955, with denser infill from the 1960s and 70s filling in behind it. The lots are narrow and the setbacks shallow, so on plenty of blocks there is no canopy at all and the roofline and the rear wall hold heat long after the sun drops. Those walls are brick veneer and hollow block, which store heat instead of shedding it. Attics over the older cottages are thinly insulated, and the air handlers tucked into them spend the day fighting that heat before a single room gets cold air.
commonCalls: A unit that has been repaired twice instead of replaced, now giving up on the hottest afternoons
Condensers with no shade, the back wall of the house reflecting heat straight into the coil
Cooling installed in the 1960s that still serves a house which has since gained a family room
Air handlers in low attic closets where the duct drop is short and the return air is starved
Second systems added years apart that fight each other when both switch on together

faqs.q: My house has been repaired for years. Is it time for a new system?
faqs.a: Age alone does not decide it. What matters is how many times the same components have been replaced and whether the outdoor unit, the air handler and the coil are all the same generation. A unit that has needed three repairs in four summers is telling you something different from one that needed a capacitor once in six years. We send your request to a company that already works Third Ward, and that company can read the nameplates and tell you which group this falls into.

faqs.q: Why is my house so much hotter than the one across the street?
faqs.a: Two houses on the same block can sit very differently. One may have a mature tree shading the west wall while the other has bare roof and brick veneer cooking in the afternoon. Solid masonry walls also hold heat into the evening after the air cools off, so the house keeps warming while the air outside drops. That is a heat load problem before it is an equipment problem, and no amount of refrigerant will fix a wall that is absorbing the afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I move the outdoor unit to a different part of the yard?
faqs.a: Often yes, and it is one of the more effective changes on a sunny lot. Moving the condenser out of the reflected heat of a brick wall, or into any shade at all, lets the unit move heat more easily. Some blocks carry historic designation, and a visible exterior change like a new condenser location or a screen wall may need review before the work starts. The technician who does the work can tell you what the local process requires.

faqs.q: Does a narrow lot leave room for a proper central system?
faqs.a: It leaves less room, but it is workable. Options usually include a compact rooftop or side yard condenser, a line set routed through an existing chase, or ductless heads on a room by room basis when there is no attic worth running duct through. The constraint on these older cottages is space for the equipment and the path to it, so the layout has to be walked before anything gets quoted.

faqs.q: Why is the same repair priced differently from one block to the next in Third Ward?
faqs.a: What is behind the wall changes what the work involves. A house framed in the 1930s with hollow block walls holds its temperature differently from a 1960s infill whose cooling was added on top of a lighter shell, and the duct runs in the two do not fail the same way. A second system added years later brings its own parts and its own age into the job, and the review process on blocks that carry historic designation changes the calendar too. So the quote moves with the house, not with the street.

faqs.q: My attic is nearly as hot as the outside. Does that affect the cooling?
faqs.a: It does, and it is the part of these houses that is hardest to see. The attics over the older cottages between Jefferson Street and Milby Street are thinly insulated, so on a clear afternoon the air up there is close to outdoor temperature, and the air handler tucked into a low closet has to pull its return air through that heat before a single room gets cold. Any duct run passing through it works against the system the whole way. Where the attic space allows it, adding insulation and sealing the duct is the least expensive improvement available, and where it does not, the sizing calculation has to account for that gain.
